evidence.excerpt:
Long-term memory is essential for language agents to main-
tain coherent and effective behavior over extended, multi-
session interactions. Existing memory systems mainly use
retrieval at read time, while write-time memory formation still
relies on direct extraction or compression. However, when
future information needs are unknown, compressing an entire
interaction in one pass can overlook locally important de-
tails that may matter later. To this end, we introduceRIME,
a retrieval-induced memory framework that shifts memory
construction from monolithic compression toward evidence-
centered integration. RIME uses generic self-questions to
retrieve focused dialogue evidence and grounds memory
formation in both the retrieved evidence and relevant histor-
ical memories, which are jointly reconciled into an evolving
memory bank with temporal and provenance information.
At inference time,

reconciliation.Given the re-
called current-session evidenceE t and the retrieved historical
memoriesH t, RIME performs fact extraction, within-session
deduplication, reference resolution, and historical reconcilia-
tion jointly in a single LLM call:
Ot =F mem (Et,H t).(9)
Each predicted operationo∈O t takes one of four forms:
op(o)∈{ADD,UPDATE,DELETE,NOOP}.(10)
ADDcreates a new memory, UPDATErevises or augments
an existing memory describing the same underlying fact,
DELETEremoves a memory explicitly contradicted as erro-
neous, and NOOPis used when the historical memory already
captures the current evidence. Each memory also retains its
temporal information and dialogue provenance.
Finally, the predicted operations are applied to obtain the
updated memory bank:
Mt = Apply (Mt−1,O t).(11)

comparable setting, we use 1,540 questions from four cate-

excluding the adversarial category.Baselines.We compare
RIME with RAG [18], Mem0 [4], A-MEM [5], Nemori [6],
and D-Mem [7], covering retrieval-based, structured, adap-
tive, and deliberative long-term memory systems.Models.

evidence.excerpt:
Table 1 compares RIME with representative long-term mem-
ory systems under two LLM backbones. RIME consistently
achieves the best performance across all three quality met-
rics with both Qwen3-235B-A22B and GPT-5.6 Sol. No-
tably, these gains are achieved with substantially lower query-
time LLM cost than deliberative memory baselines such as
A-MEM and Nemori, demonstrating that selective access to
source dialogue provides an effective alternative to expensive
deliberation over long histories.

Table 1 compares RIME with representative long-term mem-
ory systems under two LLM backbones. RIME consistently
achieves the best performance across all three quality met-
rics with both Qwen3-235B-A22B and GPT-5.6 Sol. No-
tably, these gains are achieved with substantially lower query-
time LLM cost than deliberative memory baselines such as
A-MEM and Nemori, demonstrating that selective access to
source dialogue provides an effective alternative to expensive
deliberation over long histories.

question-specific retrieval. RIME instead uses these
questions as retrieval cues before memory consolidation. As
shown in Table 2, adding the six dimensions to the compres-
sion prompt yields no consistent gain over direct compres-
sion, whereas RIME improves all three metrics. This suggests
that question-guided memory formation is effective.
Effect of selective source retrieval.We further examine
whether access to the source dialogue is necessary when se-
mantic memory is insufficient. Disabling selective source
retrieval causes a substantial performance drop on both back-
bones, with the Judge score decreasing by 10.59 points on
Qwen3-235B-A22B and 3.32 points on GPT-5.6 Sol. Source
retrieval is triggered more frequently with Qwen than with
GPT-5.6 (16.8% vs. 6.0%), consistent with the larger degra-
dation observed when this mechanism is removed.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Token F1 and BLEU-1 are external lexical-overlap metrics that corroborate the LLM-Judge quality gains across both backbones.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: LoCoMo answer quality scores are measured with an LLM Judge, token F1, and BLEU-1 against dialogue-derived reference answers.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: RIME is an untrained architectural memory pipeline that uses fixed generic formation questions, frozen text embeddings, and TF-IDF retrieval without task-specific parameter optimization.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims regarding superior memory quality, reduced query-time token costs compared to deliberative baselines, and the modular importance of write-time retrieval and read-time fallback are well supported by experimental tables.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The framework is evaluated on the standard LoCoMo benchmark (1,540 non-adversarial questions) across two LLM backbones against relevant baselines (RAG, Mem0, A-MEM, Nemori, D-Mem), measuring LLM-Judge, F1, BLEU-1, and inference tokens alongside comprehensive ablations.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Standard n-gram lexical overlap metrics (token F1 and BLEU-1) objectively corroborate the LLM-Judge quality improvements across both backbones.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: LoCoMo evaluation scores measuring answer accuracy using an LLM Judge, F1 score, and BLEU-1 against reference dialogue answers.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: The memory system is an untuned architectural pipeline using fixed generic prompt queries, frozen text embeddings, and TF-IDF without learned task-specific parameter optimization.

primary.limitations: The evaluation excludes the adversarial split of LoCoMo and relies on a fixed set of six generic formation queries, while write-time token overhead during memory construction is not explicitly quantified alongside query tokens.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is clearly specified with explicit mathematical formulations for question-guided retrieval, context expansion, memory bank operations (ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, NOOP), and fallback source dialogue retrieval via TF-IDF.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript presents a clear, well-scoped architectural contribution to LLM agent memory systems with sound technical details and rigorous comparative benchmarking against standard baselines.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces RIME, a long-term dialogue memory framework for LLM agents that uses generic question-guided evidence retrieval prior to memory consolidation and selective source-dialogue fallback at query time.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript presents a clear, well-scoped architectural contribution to LLM agent memory systems with sound technical details and rigorous comparative benchmarking against standard baselines.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The evaluation excludes the adversarial split of LoCoMo and relies on a fixed set of six generic formation queries, while write-time token overhead during memory construction is not explicitly quantified alongside query tokens.
